title: True and firm
hook: after the Shema comes "true", affirming what was said
carry: more than a dozen words, all saying yes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third paragraph, tzitzit, the fringes, and the Exodus. Your line was remember twice a day. Did you look at your reminder morning and night? Today, the word that comes the instant the Shema ends. Day five hundred seventy.

A friend has just told you something big. You listened to the whole thing, and when they finish, there's a beat of silence, and then you say: that's true. Or: I believe you. It changes what just happened. Their words are no longer only theirs; you've signed your name next to them. The Shema has just finished: three paragraphs, from Deuteronomy and Numbers. And before anyone takes a breath, the prayer book puts one word right on its heels, so close that there isn't supposed to be a pause at all. True.
screen: `A FRIEND TELLS YOU SOMETHING BIG.` → `THAT'S TRUE.` → `NO PAUSE AT ALL.`

segments.voice: The Shema ends: I am the LORD your God. And the next word is emet, true. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says not to pause between them. Tradition finds the pairing in the prophet Jeremiah. In the old Jewish translation: "But the LORD God is the true God." So the end of the Shema and the first word after it make one sentence: the LORD your God is true. Then the morning blessing carries on: emet v'yatziv, true and firm. And it doesn't stop at two. True and firm, established and lasting, right and faithful, beloved and cherished, delightful and pleasant, awesome and mighty, well-ordered and accepted, good and beautiful, is this word to us forever. More than a dozen words, piled up, all saying yes. It's a very old prayer. The Mishnah, in tractate Tamid, lists the words the priests said each morning in the Temple, and among them is emet v'yatziv. The Talmud even says that someone who didn't say emet v'yatziv in the morning, and its evening partner, emet ve'emunah, true and faithful, hasn't fulfilled their duty. Why so much insistence on this one word? Because, in the prayer's order, hearing isn't the end. The Shema says hear. Then emet answers: I heard, and I hold it to be true. That's the word's job here: not only saying the words, but standing behind them.
screen: `THE LORD YOUR GOD IS TRUE.` · `NO PAUSE BETWEEN THEM.` · `WORD AFTER WORD, ALL SAYING YES.` · `SAID IN THE TEMPLE EACH MORNING.` · then, large: `TRUE AND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say true to something you believe. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you hold to be true, deep down. Not an opinion about the news. Something you'd stand behind: that kindness matters, that your child is good, that you'll be all right, a line of scripture, a promise you made. Say it to yourself in one sentence. Then, out loud, quietly, say: true. Notice what it's like to put your weight behind it. If doubt comes, let it come, and see what's still standing. The bell holds the time.
Emet v'Yatziv. True and firm: the blessing right after the morning Shema, answering what was heard with yes.
Your line: more than a dozen words, all saying yes. Today, when you agree with someone, say so clearly, and when you say something, make sure you can stand behind it. Day five hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Right after the last words of the Shema, the prayer leader and congregation say emet, joining it without a pause, and the morning blessing Emet v'Yatziv follows; in the evening the parallel blessing is Emet ve'Emunah.

what a scholar hears: Berakhot 14a–b joins the Shema's last words to emet without a pause; the link to Jeremiah 10:10 is drawn in the tradition (see the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 2); Mishnah Tamid 5:1 has the priests saying emet v'yatziv; Berakhot 12a requires it.

sources.quoted: But the LORD God is the true God

notes: Jeremiah 10:10 opening quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Berakhot 14a–b: no pause between 'Adonai Eloheichem' and 'emet', derived from Jeremiah 10:10 (Rabbi Abbahu / Rabbi Yochanan); confirm.
Mishnah Tamid 5:1: priests recite emet v'yatziv among the morning texts; confirm.
Berakhot 12a: whoever did not say emet v'yatziv in the morning and emet ve'emunah at night has not fulfilled the obligation; confirm.
Synonym list paraphrased from the standard text; 'more than a dozen' left vague deliberately.
